newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bunds and futures stumble lower in late trade.
newsitem.headline: Bunds and futures stumble lower in late trade.

text.p: German Bunds and futures tripped up in late trade, wiping out the moderate gains clocked up earlier in the session.

Traders said the negative pull from the U.S. -- where conerns about strong factory orders data and persistent interest rate fears were haunting the Treasury market -- was too hard for Bunds to resist.
By 1440 GMT the DTB Bund futures contact was trading 14 basis points lower at 99.33, well down from its earlier daily high at 99.71.

"We can't decouple from the U.S. market as long as there are still interest rate fears there," said one Frankfurt-based trader. "But the speculation that there is any chance of a rate easing in Germany is completely off the wall."
While Bunds started the day in a reasonably chirpy mood after a recovery in Treasuries overnight, they tripped up later when T-bonds opened flat and took a swift downturn.

Traders said the fall was sparked by comments from Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer, who told the Washington Post newspaper that the U.S. economy was "really strong" and that its performance was "not a fluke".
Both cash Bunds and futures followed Treasuries into the red, with the 10-year cash yield nudging above the important 6.00 percent level.
By 1500 GMT, the 10-year was yielding 6.013 percent, trading at 99.84.

While players said the German Bund market was still looking relatively good amidst the gloom of tumbling European stock markets and jittery U.S. Treasuries, they said upside would remain limited over the next few sessions.
"I'd still be more negative than anything else," said one. "People in the market are very nervous."
In the cash market, the 10-year yield spread of Bunds to T-notes stood at 101 basis points by 1506 GMT, unchanged from Tuesday's closing levels.
Traders noted that within the German market, the 10-year area had held up relatively well, with players selling more paper at the shorter end in a bid to flatten the yield curve.
"The curve is far too steep. So I can understand wny people would be putting on flattening trades," said one.
With the all-important U.S. payrolls report due on Friday, volumes were likely to remain thin in the next few sessions, traders said.
Analysts polled by Reuters predict that 187,000 jobs will have been added to the U.S. non-farms payroll in March compared with a 339,000 rise in February.
